Cognate with {{cog|de|entgegen|t=contrary to}}, {{cog|frr|ijen|t=against}}, {{cog|da|igen||again}}, {{cog|sv|igen||again}}, and {{cog|nb|igjen||again}}{{,}} and {{cog|is|í gegnum|t=through}}. {{surf|en|on-|gain|t2=against}}. ===Pronunciation=== * {{IPA|en|/əˈɡɛn/|/əˈɡeɪn/|a=RP,CA}} ** {{audio|en|En-uk-again.ogg|a=UK}} * {{IPA|en|/əˈɡɛn/|a=GA}} ** {{audio|en|en-us-again.ogg|a=California}} *** {{IPA|en|/əˈɡɪn/|a=Southern US,AAVE,pin-pen|ref={{R:en:PEAS|5.2|131}}}} * {{IPA|en|/əˈɡæɪ̯n/|/əˈɡen/|a=AU,NZ}} * {{IPA|en|/eɪ̯ˈɡeɪ̯n/|a=dated}} * {{hyph|en|a|gain}} * {{rhymes|en|eɪn|ɛn|s=2}} ===Adverb=== {{wikidata lexeme|L3238}} {{en-adv|-}} # Another time: {{n-g|indicating a repeat of an action}}. {{defdate|from 14thc.}} #: {{ux|en|I enjoyed it so much I went '''again''' the next day.}} #* {{quote-journal|en|date=30 October 2010|author=Simon Hattenstone|journal=The Guardian |passage=The last sentence is so shocking, I have to read it '''again'''.}} # [[back|Back]] (to a former place or state). {{defdate|from 11thc.}} #: {{ux|en|We need to bring the old customs to life '''again'''.}} #: {{ux|en|The South will rise '''again'''.}} #* {{RQ:Churchill Celebrity|chapter=8|passage=The humor of my proposition appealed more strongly to Miss Trevor than I had looked for, and from that time forward she became her old self '''again''';{{...}}. Our table in the dining-room became '''again''' the abode of scintillating wit and caustic repartee, Farrar bracing up to his old standard, and the demand for seats in the vicinity rose to an animated competition.}} #* {{RQ:Lincoln Pratt's Patients|chapter=1|passage=Thinks I to myself, “Sol, you're run off your course again. This is a rich man's summer ‘cottage’{{nb...}}.{{nb...}}.” So I started to back away '''again''' into the bushes. But I hadn't backed more'n a couple of yards when I see something so amazing that I couldn't help scooching down behind the bayberries and looking at it.}} #* {{RQ:Allingham China Governess|chapter=19|passage=Meanwhile Nanny Broome was recovering from her initial panic and seemed anxious to make up for any kudos she might have lost, by exerting her personality to the utmost. She took the policeman's helmet and placed it on a chair, and unfolded his tunic to shake it and fold it up '''again''' for him.}} # Over and above a factor of one. {{defdate|from 16thc.}} #: {{ux|en|This stick is quite long, but that other one is half as long '''again'''. |q=''1½ times as long}} #* {{quote-journal|en|date=December 10 1908|author={{w|Austin Hobart Clark|Austin H. {{non-gloss|Used metalinguistically, with the repetition being in the discussion, or in the linguistic or pragmatic context of the discussion, rather than in the subject of discussion.}} ==English==

===Etymology===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*weyd-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|visiten}}, from {{der|en|fro|visiter}}, from {{der|en|la|vīsitō}}, frequentative of {{m|la|vīsō||behold, survey}}, from {{m|la|videō||see}}.<ref>{{R:OED Online|pos=v|id=1871746711}}</ref> Cognate with {{cog|osx|wīsōn|t=to visit, afflict}}, archaic {{cog|de|weisen|t=to visit, afflict}}. Displaced native {{ncog|ang|sēċan||to visit}} and {{m|ang|sōcn||a visit}}.

The noun is from {{bor|en|fr|visite}} or the verb.<ref>{{R:OED Online|pos=n|id=7308969320}}</ref> {{doublet|en|visite}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/ˈvɪzɪt/}}
* {{audio|en|en-us-visit.ogg|a=US}}
* {{rhymes|en|ɪzɪt|s=2}}
* {{hyphenation|en|vis|it}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To habitually [[go]] to (someone in distress, sickness etc.) to [[comfort]] them. (Now generally merged into later senses, below.) {{defdate|from 13th c.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|intransitive}} To go and [[meet]] (a person) as an act of [[friendliness]] or [[sociability]]. {{defdate|from 14th c.}}
#: {{ux|en|She decided to '''visit''' her grandparents for Christmas.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} Of God: to [[appear]] to (someone) to [[comfort]], [[bless]], or [[chastise]] or [[punish]] them. (Now generally merged into later senses, below.) {{defdate|from 13th c.}}
#* {{RQ:KJV|Luke|1|68|passage=[God] hath '''visited''' and redeemed his people.}}
#* {{RQ:King James Version|Ruth|1|6|passage=Then she arose with her daughters in law, that she might return from the country of Moab: for she had heard in the country of Moab how that the {{smallcaps|Lord}} had '''visited''' his people in giving them bread.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|now|rare}} To [[punish]], to inflict [[harm]] {{m|en|upon}} (someone or something). {{defdate|from 14th c.}}
#* {{RQ:Gibbon Roman Empire|volume=68
|passage=Her life was spared by the clemency of the emperor, but he '''visited''' the pomp and treasures of her palace.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} Of a sickness, misfortune etc.: to [[afflict]] (someone). {{defdate|from 14th c.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1890|author=w:James George Frazer|title=w:The Golden Bough
|passage=There used to be a sharp contest as to where the effigy was to be made, for the people thought that the house from which it was carried forth would not be '''visited''' with death that year.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To inflict [[punishment]], [[vengeance]] for (an offense) {{m|en|on}} or {{m|en|upon}} someone. {{defdate|from 14th c.}}
#* {{quote-video game|en|developer=Bungie|authorlink=Bungie|title=w:Halo 3|publisher=w:Microsoft Game Studios|date=25 September 2007|system=w:Xbox 360|level=[https://www.halopedia.org/Terminal_(Halo_3)#The_terminals Terminal Six (Legendary)]|passage=05-032 was right about one thing: there is only one way to defeat the enemy, and that is to '''visit''' utter annihilation on it.}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|author=John Mullan|journal=The Guardian|date=2 Dec 2011
|passage=If this were an Ibsen play, we would be thinking of the sins of one generation being '''visited''' upon another, he said.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To go to (a shrine, temple etc.) for [[worship]]. (Now generally merged into later senses, below.) {{defdate|from 14th c.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[go]] to (a place) for pleasure, on an errand, etc. {{defdate|from 15th c.}}
#* {{RQ:Maxwell Mirror and the Lamp|chapter=19|passage=Nothing was too small to receive attention, if a supervising eye could suggest improvements likely to conduce to the common welfare. Mr. Gordon Burnage, for instance, personally '''visited''' dust-bins and back premises, accompanied by a sort of village bailiff, going his round like a commanding officer doing billets.}}
#* {{quote-web|en|year=2018|url=https://learningenglish.voanews.com/a/china-s-melting-glacier-brings-visitors-concern-over-climate-change/4627742.html|title=VOA Learning English > China's Melting Glacier Brings Visitors, Adds to Climate Concerns
|site=learningenglish.voanews.com
|passage=Each year, millions of people '''visit''' the 4,570-meter-high Baishui Glacier in southern China.  [[File:Each year, millions of people visit.ogg]]}}

==English==

===Etymology===
From {{inh|en|enm|quykly}}, {{m|enm|quikliche}}, {{m|enm|quicliche}}, {{m|enm|cwikliche}}, {{m|enm|cwickliche}}, from {{inh|en|ang|cwiculīċe}}. {{surf|en|quick|-ly|id2=adverbial}}.

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/ˈkwɪk.li/}}
* {{audio|en|en-us-quickly.ogg|a=US}}
* {{rhymes|en|ɪkli|s=2}}

===Adverb===
{{en-adv|er,more}}

# {{1|rapidly}}; with [[speed]]; [[fast]]; with expedition.
#: {{syn|en|at speed|apace|lickety-split|q3=informal}}
#: {{ux|en|Luckily, the error was '''quickly''' corrected.}}
# Very [[soon]].
#: {{ux|en|If we go this way, we'll get there '''quickly'''.}}
#* {{RQ:en:CNN|author=Patrick Noack|title=Humans are terrible at planning for the future: Here's how we can change that|url=https://www.cnn.com/2023/02/02/opinions/patrick-noack-future-long-term-thinking-spc-intl|date=2023-02-02|passage=There are eight principles in all, but three are really important if we want to shift '''quickly''' and inclusively toward a longer-term mode of thinking and acting.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20230303181247/https://www.cnn.com/2023/02/02/opinions/patrick-noack-future-long-term-thinking-spc-intl/}}

====Usage notes====
* Although the comparative ([[quicklier]]) and superlative ([[quickliest]]) one-word forms exist and are and have been in limited use, the two-word forms (''more quickly'' and ''most quickly'') are much more common.
